summary: Gathers what is needed to introduce domain-style names across the DDN/MILNET Internet community. It gives an overview of moving from host tables to domains, a timetable for the move, and references to related documents and software, as an aid for implementors and administrators.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of one giant list of every computer's name, the network moved to a system where names are split into parts. This memo is the moving plan.

questions: how did milnet move to domain names
what was the transition from host tables to dns
when was the host table discontinued
subtitle: The plan for moving MILNET hosts from a central host table to domain-style names.

tldr.problem: Every MILNET host needs to turn other hosts' names into addresses, but the NIC's central host table had reached the limits of manageability.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes a three-stage migration from the host table to the domain system, a timetable ending with the host table being discontinued in October 1989, and a guide to the documents and software involved.
tldr.outcome: It is a transition aid for implementors and administrators, not a protocol specification. Hosts that did not convert would have to get a host table equivalent by private arrangement after the host table ended.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 1031 as Unknown, with no recorded obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a transition plan tied to dates in 1987 to 1989, and the protocols it points to are in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

sections.title: Why Move Away From the Host Table
sections.content:
All MILNET hosts need a way to translate the name of any other host into its Internet address. The existing method was a table of all hosts, maintained by the Network Information Center (NIC). Hosts fetched it by FTP, processed it locally and scanned it. The RFC says the table's size and update frequency had reached the limits of manageability, and that it relied on a central point of information.

The domain system does the same job with a distributed database. Host resolvers query domain servers, may cache answers, and each server holds a portion of a hierarchical database under separate administrative authority. Redundancy comes from transferring data between cooperating servers.

The memo reports that the domain system had operated successfully on the ARPANET for over a year, to the point that the NIC's host table was no longer a complete list. On MILNET, host names had already been converted from a flat namespace to structured names, as required by DDN Management Bulletin #32 (22 Jan 1987), and root servers had been put in place. The next step was for hosts to stop depending on the host table.
sections.plainLanguage: One giant list got too big and changed too often. So the job of knowing names was shared out among many helpers, each looking after one piece.

sections.title: The Three Migration Stages
sections.content:
Hosts would not all switch at once, so the RFC describes three stages that exist side by side as hosts convert.

  • Host table only. The host depends entirely on the NIC's table and does local table scanning. Most hosts were in this stage. Hosts that cannot ever convert (older architectures, unchangeable software) will need to get the table equivalent from another host under a bilateral agreement, a community-of-interest repository, or a locally maintained table, because the NIC will stop maintaining the table at the end of the conversion period.
  • Domain system and host table. The host uses both. A likely case is TELNET and FTP using the domain system while MAIL still uses the host table, or the reverse. This stage is viewed as transitory.
  • Domain system only. Conversion is complete, including correct handling of the mailbox and mail exchanger resource records.
sections.plainLanguage: Some houses switch to the new system first, some use both for a while, and some switch last. Nobody has to move on the same day.

sections.title: The Migration Timetable
sections.content:
The RFC gives a timetable. Operational testing of the root server software ran from December 1986 to July 1987 and had been completed. A policy was to be announced in a DDN Management Bulletin in October 1987. Host conversion would run from October 1987 to October 1989, and the host table would be discontinued in October 1989.

Voluntary conversion could begin immediately, with mandatory conversion required by October 1989. After that date, hosts that had not converted must obtain the host table equivalent by private arrangement.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone gets about two years to switch. After that date the old giant list stops being handed out.

sections.title: The Documents Behind the Domain System
sections.content:
The domain system is documented in a set of RFCs available from the NIC. The memo gives a short synopsis of each.

  • RFC 799: an early, exploratory description of name domain concepts.
  • RFC 819: a think piece on hierarchical naming aligned with administrative rather than topological boundaries.
  • RFC 920: policy on establishing a new domain, and the limited set of top level domains.
  • RFC 921: the implementation schedule of the ARPA Internet domain system.
  • RFC 952 and RFC 953: the host table format and the TCP-based Hostname Server Protocol.
  • RFC 974: how mailers route messages using mail exchanger records.
  • RFC 1032 and RFC 1033: guides for domain administrators.
  • RFC 1034 and RFC 1035: the concepts and facilities, and the implementation specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is a reading list: which other papers explain the ideas, the rules, and how to build and run the new system.

sections.title: Available Implementations
sections.content:
So that vendors could inspect working code, the memo lists several domain system implementations. The two most mature are JEEVES, a TOPS-20 server and resolver run by some ARPANET root servers and maintained at ISI, and BIND, the 4BSD Unix resolver and server run by most lower-level domain servers on the ARPANET and maintained at UC Berkeley. A commercial BIND shipped with Sun Microsystems' operating system version 3.2.

Others listed include a MS-DOS port of BIND from FTP Software, resolvers for TOPS-20 and ITS, Symbolics Lisp machines, Xerox Cedar, the Harris H series, Multics and VAX/VMS, and server and resolver code for Fuzzballs and the Macintosh. Some are partial: the VAX/VMS resolver supports only address queries and IN-ADDR PTR lookups, and the Fuzzball code does not support zone transfers. The memo lists points of contact for each.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists who already built working versions of the new system for different kinds of computers, so others can look at their work.
